title: Everyone who thirsts (Isaiah 55:1–11)
hookLine: come, buy without money; my word shall not return empty

cards: A market in an ancient city. Stalls of bread and dates, sacks of grain, jars of wine, goat's milk in skins. Sellers shouting over each other: over here, best price, come and buy.
Then one voice cuts through the noise with an offer nobody else is making. Come and buy, it says, but you don't need money. Bring nothing.
Take wine and milk anyway. Free. In a market, that sounds either like a trick or like madness.
Isaiah puts it in God's mouth.

teach.h: HO! A CRY ACROSS THE MARKET.
teach.b: It opens, in the King James Bible: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."
Ho is a cry for attention, the kind you'd hear across a market: hey, over here!

teach.h: WHY SPEND ON WHAT ISN'T BREAD?
teach.b: Water, then wine and milk: from what keeps you alive to what makes a feast. Then a question that still lands: "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?"
Why spend your paycheck, your hours, your attention, on things that don't fill you? Listen, God says, and eat what is good. Seek the Lord while he may be found.

teach.h: MY WAYS ARE NOT YOUR WAYS.
teach.b: Then a line people quote when nothing makes sense: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD." As high as the heavens are above the earth. Then a picture from farming.
Rain and snow don't go back up empty. They water the earth, make it sprout, give seed to the sower and bread to the eater.
"So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void." In the poem, God's word works like rain, doing its work even before anyone sees it.

And the chapter ends in a burst: the mountains and hills break into singing, and all the trees of the field clap their hands. Christians often hear in this chapter the free gift they call grace, offered to everyone.
Jewish readers hear God's covenant love, offered again to exiles on their way home.

how: Isaiah 55 is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic and many Anglican and Lutheran churches, and Protestant preachers often use its opening as an invitation to grace; verse 8 is often turned to in times of confusion or loss.

o: a free gift from God, offered with no price
a market tax lifted for the poor on feast days
a fee paid at the Temple for forgiveness

games.q: what's inside the invitation — tap the pairs.

s: the invitation is only for those who can pay
"he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat."
Isaiah compares God's word to rain and snow
they water the earth before returning; God's word shall not return void.
the mountains sing and the trees of the field clap their hands.

games.q: you're in the market with no money, thirsty and hungry. a voice shouts, come, buy wine and milk. what's the catch?
o: there is none: without money and without price.
you must prove you deserve it first.
games.why: "come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." a sales pitch with no price: it's free.

practice: Think back over the last day, where your money, time and attention went, and without judging, notice one thing that didn't fill you.
Then notice one thing that did and cost nothing, a meal with someone, a walk, a moment of quiet, a laugh, and hold that one, along with something you could give the same way, freely, without price.
If you pray, you can give thanks for what came free.

wordCard.voice: Grace. The free gift Christians hear in Isaiah's market cry: come to the waters, and buy with no money at all.

orig.note: Hebrew: ho, everyone who thirsts! a cry for attention.
